SK Telecom's AI data center arm, SK Hyper, is seeking about $350 billion for the first 5 gigawatts of a 15 gigawatt plan in South Korea.
It is in talks with big tech companies and investors, none named yet.
The first sites are due in 2029.

threads_text: SK Telecom's data center arm wants about $350 billion, and that only pays for the first 5 of a planned 15 gigawatts in South Korea. The whole country runs on roughly 1 gigawatt of data centers today, its CEO says. Smart bet on AI demand, or a bubble in the making?

paragraphs.text: SK Hyper, the AI data center unit of South Korea's SK Telecom, is in talks with large technology companies and financial investors to fund an AI infrastructure buildout it values at about $350 billion, according to a Bloomberg report published on October 23, 2026. Chief executive Chung Suk-geun described the plan in an interview with Bloomberg Television.

The $350 billion figure, about 463 trillion won, covers only the first phase of the project: 5 gigawatts of data center capacity, including servers and other equipment, Seoul Economic Daily reported. The longer goal is 15 gigawatts of capacity in South Korea by 2035.
How the money would be raised

SK Hyper aims to close its first round of outside investment by the end of 2026 or early 2027, according to the reports, and to keep raising money over the following three to four years. The company has not named the technology firms or investors it is talking to, and no terms were disclosed.

The company intends to share project costs with data center tenants and outside investors rather than carry the full amount itself. Chung said SK Hyper would match its spending to actual demand instead of committing to the whole program at once, and that it plans to confirm demand with large technology companies before investing.

SK Telecom has said it will put up to 750 billion won, about $510 million, into SK Hyper in stages through 2030. The subsidiary was created in July 2026 as a wholly owned unit, with Chung, who also leads SK Telecom's AI company-in-company, as its first chief executive.
Where the data centers would go

The first data centers are scheduled for completion in 2029, when phased operations toward the initial 5 gigawatts would begin, Seoul Economic Daily reported. An SK AI data center in Ulsan is the starting point for a cluster of more than 2 gigawatts in the Yeongnam region, with gigawatt-scale sites also planned in the Chungcheong and southwestern regions.

For scale, Chung said South Korea's entire data center market is currently about 1 gigawatt. He said the company expects global customers to matter more than domestic ones, and the plan aims to draw AI computing demand from other Asian countries, including Japan and Taiwan. SK Hyper is also in talks with global cloud providers about AI inference hubs in Korea, according to Seoul Economic Daily.

Chung also argued that the industry's priorities have shifted. In his account, the main advantage used to be securing the most graphics processors, while the test now is which operator can produce AI output at the lowest cost and highest efficiency. He added that revenue could start as early as 2027.

The plan sits inside a wider SK Group push. Startup Fortune reported that SK Group chairman Chey Tae-won has discussed investing roughly 1,000 trillion won, about $648 billion, in AI data centers by 2035. Light Reading reported in July that the South Korean government has set a national target for AI data center capacity by 2035, with SK Group expected to develop 15 gigawatts of it.

The pitch arrives at an awkward moment. Investors have been questioning whether demand for AI services will justify the amounts being spent on computing infrastructure around the world, a concern noted in coverage of this plan. SK Hyper's answer is a project finance model in which tenants and outside investors carry much of the cost and construction follows signed demand. That structure lowers the risk for SK Telecom, but it also means the plan depends heavily on persuading foreign technology companies to place large workloads in Korea.
The first test is the outside funding round SK Hyper targets for the end of 2026 or early 2027, and whether any of the technology companies it is courting are named as tenants or investors.
